title: Year two close
hook: three hundred sixty-five sessions: seven Upanishads, the Yoga Sutras, the whole Ramayana, a year of festivals, and three paths
tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame

segments.voice: Yesterday: jnana, and Shankara's Atmabodha. Sweeping won't clear a dark room; only the light does. Was there a shadow you put the light on? Today, the last day of year two. Day six hundred ninety-six.

Three hundred sixty-five sessions ago, year two opened with a promise: the texts underneath. Not the stories people tell about Hinduism, but the old pages the stories rest on. Since then you've sat with a father telling his son, that you are. You've read a sage defining yoga in one short line. You've walked the whole Ramayana, from a bird's cry to the earth opening. You've kept a year of festivals. Today we stand at the top and look back down the slope.
screen: `THE TEXTS UNDERNEATH.` → `THREE HUNDRED SIXTY-FIVE SESSIONS.` → `LOOK BACK DOWN THE SLOPE.`

segments.voice: Four blocks. First, the seven big Upanishads: the Chandogya, the Brihadaranyaka, the Taittiriya, the Aitareya, the Prashna, the Mundaka and the Shvetashvatara. Uddalaka and the salt in the water, and his line to Shvetaketu, tat tvam asi, that you are. Gargi asking her questions like arrows. The two kinds of knowledge. Second, the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, in four parts, opening with atha, now, and then the definition: yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Third, Valmiki's Ramayana, seven books in a hundred and eighty sessions: a bow broken, sandals on a throne, a leap across the sea, a homecoming, and a later book whose ending the tradition still argues over with love. Fourth, the festival year, from Janmashtami's midnight to Shivaratri's all-night watch, and then the three strands of the lineage track. Karma, with the Isha asking the mind to remember what was done. Bhakti, with Narada's supreme love and the ache of forgetting. Jnana, with Shankara's light in the dark room. Why call it the summit of the texts? Because so much of what comes next leans on these pages. Later teachers keep returning to the Upanishads. Yoga teachers still go back to Patanjali's sutras. Poets retold Valmiki in other tongues: Kamban in Tamil, Tulsidas in Awadhi. Hindus don't all read these texts the same way, and the schools you met this week read them differently. But they read the same roots. Tomorrow, year three begins with the Mahabharata, and it opens not with a battle but with a king and a sacrifice of snakes.
screen: `SEVEN UPANISHADS: THAT YOU ARE.` · `PATANJALI: STILLING THE MIND.` · `VALMIKI: SEVEN BOOKS.` · `FESTIVALS, AND THREE PATHS.` · then, large: `YOU'VE READ THE ROOTS.`

segments.voice: Sit as if at the top of a hill, the whole year below you. Let one line from year two rise on its own: that you are, or the stilling of the mind, or remember what was done, or anything else that stayed. Don't choose; wait for it. When it comes, hold it in the breath, in on the first half, out on the second. Then let it rest, and just look out over the year. The bell holds the time.
The summit of the texts. Seven Upanishads, the Yoga Sutras, the Ramayana, the festival year, and three paths, read at the source.
screen: `THE SUMMIT OF THE TEXTS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: you've read the roots. Today, tell one person one thing from year two that surprised you. Day six hundred ninety-six, and year two is done.

howItsDone: Hindus often mark the end of a course of study, or the completion of a text, with a closing recitation, a peace chant, and an offering of thanks to the teacher. Some families sponsor a reading or feed guests when a long recitation is finished.
